steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the "Properties" section of a Wikipedia article on the analytic signal, covering instantaneous amplitude, phase and frequency, and the complex envelope (complex baseband).

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
## Instantaneous amplitude and phase
- polar form: envelope, instantaneous phase and frequency; applications
## Complex envelope/baseband
- down-conversion, choices of reference frequency and their consequences
- Wigner–Ville distribution; meanings of "complex envelope"

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
## Instantaneous amplitude and phase
- polar coordinates: s_\mathrm{a}(t) = s_\mathrm{m}(t)e^{j\phi(t)},
- s_\mathrm{m}(t) \triangleq |s_\mathrm{a}(t)|: instantaneous amplitude / envelope
- \phi(t) \triangleq \arg\!\left[s_\mathrm{a}(t)\right]: instantaneous phase / phase angle
- diagram: blue curve s(t), red curve s_\mathrm{m}(t)
- derivative of unwrapped phase = instantaneous angular frequency (radians/second): \omega(t) \triangleq \frac{d\phi}{dt}(t).
- instantaneous frequency in hertz: f(t)\triangleq \frac{1}{2\pi}\omega(t).
- uses: measuring/detecting local features; demodulation — polar form separates amplitude modulation from phase (frequency) modulation

## Complex envelope/baseband
- down-conversion toward 0 Hz, possibly [non-symmetrical] negative frequency components: {s_\mathrm{a}}_{\downarrow}(t) \triangleq s_\mathrm{a}(t)e^{-j\omega_0 t} = s_\mathrm{m}(t)e^{j(\phi(t) - \omega_0 t)},
- \omega_0 arbitrary reference angular frequency
- names: complex envelope, complex baseband; not unique, depends on \omega_0; used for passband signals; for modulated s(t), \omega_0 = carrier frequency
- or \omega_0 in middle of desired passband -> simple real low-pass filter excises portion of interest
- also reduces highest frequency -> lower minimum alias-free sampling rate
- still analytic (tractability kept), but real-valued representation not just real part: up-conversion, interpolation (upsampling) if sampled
- \omega_0 above highest frequency of s_\mathrm{a}(t): no positive frequencies; real part restores them in reverse order -> demodulate lower sideband / inverted sideband
- other choices: minimize \int_0^{+\infty}(\omega - \omega_0)^2|S_\mathrm{a}(\omega)|^2\, d\omega.; minimize mean square error of linear approximation to \phi(t): \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}[\omega(t) - \omega_0]^2 |s_\mathrm{a}(t)|^2\, dt; or (optimum \theta) \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}[\phi(t) - (\omega_0 t + \theta)]^2\, dt.
- time-frequency signal processing: analytic signal needed in Wigner–Ville distribution definition for practical properties
- "complex envelope" sometimes = complex amplitude of (constant-frequency) phasor; other times s_m(t) as time-dependent generalization of complex amplitude
- like real-valued case: varying envelope generalizes constant amplitude

steps.text:
## Instantaneous amplitude and phase

An analytic signal can also be written in polar coordinates:

s_\mathrm{a}(t) = s_\mathrm{m}(t)e^{j\phi(t)},

where we introduce the following time-variant quantities:

s_\mathrm{m}(t) \triangleq |s_\mathrm{a}(t)| is called the instantaneous amplitude or the envelope;

\phi(t) \triangleq \arg\!\left[s_\mathrm{a}(t)\right] is called the instantaneous phase or phase angle.

In the diagram, the blue curve shows s(t) and the red curve shows the corresponding s_\mathrm{m}(t) .

The time derivative of the unwrapped instantaneous phase is called the instantaneous angular frequency, and its units are radians/second:

\omega(t) \triangleq \frac{d\phi}{dt}(t).

So the instantaneous frequency (in hertz) is:

f(t)\triangleq \frac{1}{2\pi}\omega(t).

In some applications the instantaneous amplitude, phase and frequency are used to measure and detect local features of the signal. Another application of the analytic representation is the demodulation of modulated signals. The polar coordinates separate the effects of amplitude modulation and phase (or frequency) modulation in a convenient way, and this effectively demodulates some kinds of signals.

## Complex envelope/baseband

Analytic signals are often shifted in frequency toward 0 Hz (down-converted), and this can create [non-symmetrical] negative frequency components:

{s_\mathrm{a}}_{\downarrow}(t) \triangleq s_\mathrm{a}(t)e^{-j\omega_0 t} = s_\mathrm{m}(t)e^{j(\phi(t) - \omega_0 t)},

where \omega_0 is an arbitrary reference angular frequency.

This function has various names, like complex envelope and complex baseband. The complex envelope is not unique, because it depends on the choice of \omega_0 . The concept is often used for passband signals. If s(t) is a modulated signal, \omega_0 might be set equal to its carrier frequency.

- or \omega_0 in middle of desired passband -> simple real low-pass filter excises portion of interest; also reduces highest frequency -> lower minimum alias-free sampling rate
- still analytic, but real-valued representation not just the real part: up-conversion, interpolation (upsampling) if sampled
- \omega_0 above highest frequency of s_\mathrm{a}(t): {s_\mathrm{a}}_{\downarrow}(t) has no positive frequencies; real part restores them in reverse order -> demodulate lower sideband / inverted sideband
- other choices of \omega_0: minimize \int_0^{+\infty}(\omega - \omega_0)^2|S_\mathrm{a}(\omega)|^2\, d\omega.; minimize mean square error of linear approximation to \phi(t): \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}[\omega(t) - \omega_0]^2 |s_\mathrm{a}(t)|^2\, dt; or (optimum \theta) \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}[\phi(t) - (\omega_0 t + \theta)]^2\, dt.
- Wigner–Ville distribution needs the analytic signal for practical properties
- "complex envelope": complex amplitude of a (constant-frequency) phasor, or s_m(t) as time-dependent generalization; varying envelope generalizing constant amplitude

steps.text:
## Instantaneous amplitude and phase

An analytic signal can also be written in polar coordinates:

s_\mathrm{a}(t) = s_\mathrm{m}(t)e^{j\phi(t)},

where we introduce the following time-variant quantities:

s_\mathrm{m}(t) \triangleq |s_\mathrm{a}(t)| is called the instantaneous amplitude or the envelope;

\phi(t) \triangleq \arg\!\left[s_\mathrm{a}(t)\right] is called the instantaneous phase or phase angle.

In the diagram, the blue curve shows s(t) and the red curve shows the corresponding s_\mathrm{m}(t) .

The time derivative of the unwrapped instantaneous phase is called the instantaneous angular frequency, and its units are radians/second:

\omega(t) \triangleq \frac{d\phi}{dt}(t).

So the instantaneous frequency (in hertz) is:

f(t)\triangleq \frac{1}{2\pi}\omega(t).

In some applications the instantaneous amplitude, phase and frequency are used to measure and detect local features of the signal. Another application of the analytic representation is the demodulation of modulated signals. The polar coordinates separate the effects of amplitude modulation and phase (or frequency) modulation in a convenient way, and this effectively demodulates some kinds of signals.

## Complex envelope/baseband

Analytic signals are often shifted in frequency toward 0 Hz (down-converted), and this can create [non-symmetrical] negative frequency components:

{s_\mathrm{a}}_{\downarrow}(t) \triangleq s_\mathrm{a}(t)e^{-j\omega_0 t} = s_\mathrm{m}(t)e^{j(\phi(t) - \omega_0 t)},

where \omega_0 is an arbitrary reference angular frequency.

This function has various names, like complex envelope and complex baseband. The complex envelope is not unique, because it depends on the choice of \omega_0 . The concept is often used for passband signals. If s(t) is a modulated signal, \omega_0 might be set equal to its carrier frequency.

In other cases \omega_0 is chosen to be somewhere in the middle of the desired passband. Then a simple low-pass filter with real coefficients can cut out the portion of interest. Another reason for doing it is to reduce the highest frequency, which reduces the minimum rate for alias-free sampling. Shifting the frequency does not undermine the mathematical tractability of the complex signal representation, so in that sense the down-converted signal is still analytic. But getting back the real-valued representation is no longer just a matter of extracting the real component. Up-conversion may be needed, and if the signal has been sampled (discrete-time), interpolation (upsampling) might also be needed to avoid aliasing.

If \omega_0 is chosen larger than the highest frequency of s_\mathrm{a}(t), then {s_\mathrm{a}}_{\downarrow}(t) has no positive frequencies. In that case extracting the real component restores them, but in reverse order, so the low-frequency components become high ones and the other way around. This can be used to demodulate a type of single-sideband signal that is called lower sideband or inverted sideband.

Other choices of reference frequency are also sometimes considered:

Sometimes \omega_0 is chosen to minimize \int_0^{+\infty}(\omega - \omega_0)^2|S_\mathrm{a}(\omega)|^2\, d\omega.

Or \omega_0 can be chosen to minimize the mean square error of a linear approximation of the unwrapped instantaneous phase \phi(t) : \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}[\omega(t) - \omega_0]^2 |s_\mathrm{a}(t)|^2\, dt

or another alternative (for some optimum \theta ): \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}[\phi(t) - (\omega_0 t + \theta)]^2\, dt.

In time-frequency signal processing, it was shown that the analytic signal was needed in the definition of the Wigner–Ville distribution so that the method has the desirable properties that are needed for practical applications.

Sometimes "complex envelope" is given the simpler meaning of the complex amplitude of a (constant-frequency) phasor; other times the complex envelope s_m(t) defined above is interpreted as a time-dependent generalization of the complex amplitude. The relationship is similar to the real-valued case, where a varying envelope generalizes a constant amplitude.

steps.text:
## Instantaneous amplitude and phase

An analytic signal can also be expressed in polar coordinates:

s_\mathrm{a}(t) = s_\mathrm{m}(t)e^{j\phi(t)},

where the following time-variant quantities are introduced:

s_\mathrm{m}(t) \triangleq |s_\mathrm{a}(t)| is called the instantaneous amplitude or the envelope;

\phi(t) \triangleq \arg\!\left[s_\mathrm{a}(t)\right] is called the instantaneous phase or phase angle.

In the accompanying diagram, the blue curve depicts s(t) and the red curve the corresponding s_\mathrm{m}(t) .

The time derivative of the unwrapped instantaneous phase, which has units of radians/second, is called the instantaneous angular frequency:

\omega(t) \triangleq \frac{d\phi}{dt}(t).

The instantaneous frequency (in hertz) is therefore:[1]

f(t)\triangleq \frac{1}{2\pi}\omega(t).

The instantaneous amplitude, phase and frequency are used in some applications to measure and detect local features of the signal. Another application of the analytic representation of a signal relates to the demodulation of modulated signals. The polar coordinates conveniently separate the effects of amplitude modulation and phase (or frequency) modulation, and effectively demodulate certain kinds of signals.

## Complex envelope/baseband

Analytic signals are often shifted in frequency (down-converted) toward 0 Hz, possibly creating [non-symmetrical] negative frequency components:

{s_\mathrm{a}}_{\downarrow}(t) \triangleq s_\mathrm{a}(t)e^{-j\omega_0 t} = s_\mathrm{m}(t)e^{j(\phi(t) - \omega_0 t)},

where \omega_0 is an arbitrary reference angular frequency.[2]

This function goes by various names, such as complex envelope and complex baseband. The complex envelope is not unique; it is determined by the choice of \omega_0 . The concept is often used when dealing with passband signals. If s(t) is a modulated signal, \omega_0 might be equated to its carrier frequency.

In other cases, \omega_0 is selected somewhere in the middle of the desired passband, so that a simple low-pass filter with real coefficients can excise the portion of interest. Another motive is to reduce the highest frequency, which reduces the minimum rate for alias-free sampling. A frequency shift does not undermine the mathematical tractability of the complex signal representation, so in that sense the down-converted signal is still analytic. However, restoring the real-valued representation is no longer simply a matter of extracting the real component. Up-conversion may be required, and if the signal has been sampled (discrete-time), interpolation (upsampling) might also be necessary to avoid aliasing.

If \omega_0 is chosen larger than the highest frequency of s_\mathrm{a}(t), then {s_\mathrm{a}}_{\downarrow}(t) has no positive frequencies. In that case, extracting the real component restores them, but in reverse order: the low-frequency components become high ones and vice versa. This can be used to demodulate a type of single-sideband signal called lower sideband or inverted sideband.

Other choices of reference frequency are sometimes considered:

Sometimes \omega_0 is chosen to minimize \int_0^{+\infty}(\omega - \omega_0)^2|S_\mathrm{a}(\omega)|^2\, d\omega.

Alternatively,[3] \omega_0 can be chosen to minimize the mean square error in linearly approximating the unwrapped instantaneous phase \phi(t) : \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}[\omega(t) - \omega_0]^2 |s_\mathrm{a}(t)|^2\, dt

or another alternative (for some optimum \theta ): \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}[\phi(t) - (\omega_0 t + \theta)]^2\, dt.

In time-frequency signal processing, it was shown that the analytic signal is needed in the definition of the Wigner–Ville distribution for the method to have the desirable properties needed for practical applications.[4]

Sometimes the phrase "complex envelope" is given the simpler meaning of the complex amplitude of a (constant-frequency) phasor;[5,6] other times the complex envelope s_m(t) as defined above is interpreted as a time-dependent generalization of the complex amplitude.[7] The relationship is not unlike that in the real-valued case: a varying envelope generalizing a constant amplitude.

References:
[1] B. Boashash, "Estimating and Interpreting the Instantaneous Frequency of a Signal-Part I: Fundamentals", Proceedings of the IEEE, Vol. 80, No. 4, pp. 519–538, April 1992.
[2] Bracewell, Ron. The Fourier Transform and Its Applications. McGraw-Hill, 2000. pp. 361–362.
[3] Justice, J.. (1979-12-01). Analytic signal processing in music computation. IEEE Transactions on Acoustics, Speech, and Signal Processing. doi:10.1109/TASSP.1979.1163321
[4] B. Boashash, "Notes on the use of the Wigner distribution for time frequency signal analysis", IEEE Trans. on Acoustics, Speech, and Signal Processing, vol. 26, no. 9, 1987.

[6] Driggers, Ronald G.. (2003-01-01). Encyclopedia of Optical Engineering: Abe-Las, pages 1-1024. CRC Press. https://books.google.com/books?id=kxICp6t-CDAC&q=%2522complex%2520amplitude%2522%2520%2522complex%2520envelope%2522&pg=RA1-PA586
